p: Dani Ruiz is thirty four, a paralegal at the state public defender's trial office in Denver, and she's studying for the law school admission test, one question per bus stop.
On a Saturday night in October 2007, a man named Travis Hensley was hit in the back lot of a bar in Commerce City, and he died before morning.
Her father, Luis, was convicted of it the next June, and he's been in the prison at Sterling ever since. Dani was fifteen, and she was a witness at his trial.
He calls her every Wednesday at seven, and she takes the call on the basement stairs of the house she grew up in.
The people you'll hear from first.
Teo Ruiz. Dani's younger brother, a diesel mechanic at a bus garage.
Luis Ruiz. Dani's father, nineteen years into a forty year sentence.
Joel Harlan. The supervising attorney on Dani's floor at the public defender's office.
Ana Brennan. A lawyer who works alone, upstairs from a laundromat on Federal Boulevard.

Tuesday, October 27, the 6:52 bus into downtown was warm and half empty, and Dani Ruiz had the back seat to herself. She had a used LSAT prep book open on her knees. It had cost six dollars online and came with somebody else's coffee ring on the cover and somebody else's pencil marks all through chapter three. She'd erased most of them.

She was thirty four, a paralegal for eight years at the Denver trial office of the state public defender, and she was registered for the January test, eleven weeks out. She'd counted. She did one question per stop, a rule she'd made up in September and mostly kept. Read the stem. Read the argument. Find the conclusion before anything else. The book said that on every page, in bold, like it didn't trust her.
Somewhere past the rail yards the next one came up.

Practice question, page 214. A witness saw a person in a red coat leave the Linden Street pharmacy a few minutes before the theft was discovered. Oren Talley was in the pharmacy that afternoon, and Talley owns a red coat. Talley also argued with the pharmacist last spring. So Talley is the person the witness saw, and it follows that Talley committed the theft. The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument...

She read it once. A coat, a pharmacy, a man with a grudge. Easy. She uncapped her highlighter and then stopped, because the book's rule was the conclusion first, and this one had two places near the end that both sounded like the end.
Ana's Pencil: start at the end.

Dicta's asleep on the rug, which means it's after six and the dryers downstairs have started on the evening loads. Good. Sharpen a pencil. We're going to do the one thing I care about, and we're going to do it every single time.

Every argument on this test is a claim and some reasons. The claim is the conclusion. The reasons are premises. You find the conclusion first, before you judge anything, because you can't say what's wrong with a road until you know where it goes. Try this one. The dryers on the left are faster. I ran a load in each on Saturday, and the left one was dry in thirty eight minutes and the right one took fifty. So the owner should put the big loads on the left.

Ask each sentence one question: why should I believe that? If the argument answers you, the sentence is a conclusion. If it just sits there as given, it's a premise. The thirty eight minutes is given. "The left ones are faster" gets answered by the thirty eight minutes, so it's a conclusion, but it isn't the end. It's there to hold up the last sentence. That makes it an intermediate conclusion. The main conclusion is the claim nothing else in the argument is there to support.

Indicator words help, and they lie. Words like "so," "thus," and "therefore" usually point at a conclusion. Words like "because," "since," and "given that" usually point at a premise. Usually. A conclusion can come first. It can hide in the middle, right after a "but." When an argument opens with what other people think, the author's own conclusion is often the sentence that turns on them.

Stuck between two claims? Put "therefore" between them, one way and then the other. The order that sounds like reasoning tells you which one is the conclusion. The thirty eight minutes, therefore the left dryers are faster. Yes. The left dryers are faster, therefore thirty eight minutes. No.

How the exam asks it. Main conclusion stems ask which choice most accurately expresses the conclusion or the main point. The traps are a premise, the intermediate conclusion, and a choice that says more than the author said. Match the author's claim at the author's strength.

The test will also point at one sentence and ask what it does. It doesn't care what the sentence says. It cares what job the sentence has. There are only a few jobs. Main conclusion. Premise. Intermediate conclusion, which takes support from one claim and gives it to another. Background, which sets the scene and proves nothing. Or the other side: a view the author is about to knock down, and sometimes the evidence for that view.

Do it in pencil. Bracket the main conclusion. Draw an arrow from each reason to whatever it holds up. Then find the sentence the question named and look at its arrows. Arrows coming in and going out means intermediate. Only going out means premise. Only coming in means main conclusion. No arrows usually means background, unless it's the view the author is knocking down.
The trap I see most: the right answer describes the job, and the wrong ones describe the content, accurately, which is why they're tempting. "It reports how fast the dryer was" is true and useless.

How the exam asks it. Role questions quote a claim and ask what role it plays. Name the job before you read the choices. Check both directions: what supports this claim, and what does this claim support?

Sometimes the argument stops and leaves a blank, usually right after "so" or "thus." That blank is a conclusion, and your job is to write the one the premises actually earn. Not the one you'd like. Not the one that sounds brave.

Finish it yourself, in plain words, before you look at the choices. Then pick the choice that says what you said, at that strength. Watch for the answer that goes one step past the evidence. If the premises show that a description fits a whole group, the blank says the description can't pick out one member of it. It doesn't say who's innocent. Breaking an argument doesn't prove the opposite. If you take one sentence from me this year, take that one.

How the exam asks it. The stem asks which choice most logically completes the argument. After "so" or "therefore," the blank is the conclusion. After "because" or "since," it's a premise that has to close the gap. Wrong answers run too strong, bring in something new, or point the other way.
Most of this test lives in the space between the reasons and the claim, and you can't see that space until you know where the claim is.

If the conclusion needs something the premises never said, the missing piece is an assumption. A necessary assumption is one the argument can't survive without. Test it by denying it: if the denial wrecks the argument, it was necessary. We'll spend next chapter in that gap.

Sometimes the gap has a familiar shape, and that's a flaw. A description that fits a whole group gets treated as if it fit one member. A change that came after something gets credited to it. Say what the argument took for granted, in the argument's own terms.

And some stimuli have no conclusion at all. They're just facts, and the question asks what those facts most strongly support. Don't add anything. Pick the modest claim the facts make likely, and be suspicious of words like "all," "always," and "proves."

How the exam asks it. Flaw stems ask why the reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism. Necessary assumption stems ask what the argument depends on or requires. Most strongly supported stems want what the facts back, not what they merely allow.

Reading Comprehension gives you a passage of four or five hundred words and a set of five to eight questions. Read it like an argument with paragraphs. Who's talking? What do they claim? What is each paragraph for?

The main idea covers the whole passage, not one paragraph and not more than the passage says. The primary purpose is the main idea as a verb: to argue, to describe, to challenge, to ask. A detail question has its answer in a line you can put your finger on, so go back and find the line. Don't answer from memory. A function question asks why the author put something there, like to support a claim, give an example, or answer an objection.
And stay inside the page. If the passage doesn't say it, you don't know it, whatever else you know.

One set in each Reading Comprehension section usually pairs two shorter passages on the same subject, and some of its questions ask how the two relate. The subjects run from law to science to history and the arts, and you don't need to know any of it going in.

And practice on the real thing, too. LSAC runs a site called LawHub with real PrepTests, old tests it gave and then released, a few for free and a lot more in a paid library. Take them in the mode that times you like the real day. It has free practice for the writing part, LSAT Argumentative Writing, as well. What we do up here teaches you the moves. Those tests teach you the clock.

How the exam asks it. The test is four sections of 35 minutes: two scored Logical Reasoning, one scored Reading Comprehension, and one unscored section of either type that you can't pick out, so treat them all as scored. There's a 10 minute break after the second section and no logic games. A wrong answer costs nothing extra, so never leave one blank.

She read the argument twice. It was the kind of question she liked, because it looked hard and wasn't, and the answer key was in the back of the book where she couldn't peek without making a production of it.

The stem wanted the flaw. Before the flaw, the conclusion. Two pieces at the end sounded like endings: "Talley is the person the witness saw," and "it follows that Talley committed the theft." She held the highlighter over the page.
A. Talley owns a red coat, which is the fact the whole thing turns on.
B. A person in a red coat left the pharmacy before the theft was found.
C. Talley is the person the witness saw leave the pharmacy that day.
D. Talley committed the theft. The rest is there to get you to that.

She brackets the last clause. Then she asks the book's question of everything else: why should I believe that? The coat is a reason. The argument with the pharmacist is a reason. "Talley is the person the witness saw" is a step on the way. The end is the theft. Now she can go looking for the flaw.

That's the one. Pencil down. Main conclusion. "It follows that" flags the end. The coat and the grudge are premises, and "Talley is the person the witness saw" is an intermediate step that holds up the theft. Find the end first, and only then go looking for the flaw.

She found it two stops later and wrote it in the margin. Could be anyone in a red coat. Then she read her own handwriting back, and the pencil stayed where it was, because she knew that argument. Not from a book. From a courtroom in Brighton, with her father at the defense table, and nobody in that room had said what she'd just written.
The bus climbed onto the viaduct. She looked at the date on her phone, which she'd been not doing since she woke up.

Tuesday, October 27. Nineteen years ago it had been a Saturday. The Rockies had played the Red Sox at Coors Field, and a man named Travis Hensley had been hit in the Night Owl Tap's parking lot in Commerce City and died before morning. A neighbor across the street had seen a man in a red jacket do it. Dani's father had owned a red jacket. Dani had said so, under oath, at fifteen.

That night Teo came by for the furnace. That was what he said, the furnace. He was twenty nine, a diesel mechanic at a bus garage, and he didn't visit so much as fix things. He took his headlamp and his toolbag down to the basement of the house they grew up in, the house their mother died in, and Dani followed him down and took the banker's box off the shelf over the washer. The same washer. It still worked, mostly. Neither of them said what day it was.

Teo looked at the box on her knees, then at the shelf, then at the washer under it. You could keep that somewhere else, he said. Anywhere else. He went back into the furnace closet, and she heard him not leave.

Trial transcript, Wednesday, June 4, 2008, direct examination. Question. How old are you? Answer. Fifteen. Question. Where were you on the night of Saturday, October 27, 2007? Answer. At a birthday sleepover. In Thornton. Question. When did you come home? Answer. Sunday morning. About eight. Question. Did you see your father that morning? Answer. Yes. He was at the kitchen table. Question. Does your father own a red jacket? Answer. His work jacket. From the refinery. Question. Did he wear it Saturday? Answer. He wore it to work that day. I saw him leave in it. Question. Where was the jacket when you got home on Sunday? Answer. In the washer, downstairs. It was wet. The cycle was done. Question. Who usually does the laundry in your house? Answer. My mom. On Mondays. Question. Had you ever seen your father wash that jacket himself? Answer. No. Thank you. Nothing further.
She read her own answers twice, standing up. Then she made herself do what the book said to do with any passage: say what the whole thing says, in one sentence, before deciding anything about it.
A. Her answers show her father was the man the neighbor saw that night in the lot.
B. It shows the jacket had blood on it when she found it in the washer that morning.
C. It records where she spent Saturday night and when she got home on Sunday.
D. It puts him in the red jacket that day, and the jacket in the washer the next morning.

She writes it on a sticky note. The jacket on him that day, and in the washer the next morning. That's all she said. Fifteen years old, a page of answers, and not one of them was about a parking lot. Whatever the jury heard about the parking lot, they heard it from somebody else.

Right. Now say why. Main idea. It covers the whole excerpt at the excerpt's own scope: the jacket worn that day, found washed the next morning, outside the house's routine. Everything on the page builds toward those two facts, and nothing on it goes further.
Under the transcript there was a note in her mother's handwriting on the back of an electric bill. Dani testifies Wednesday. Bring her a sweater, the courtroom is cold.

Dani sat down on the basement stairs with it. She'd told the truth. She'd told it to a room full of strangers while her father sat at a table and didn't look at her, and every word had been true. And here was the part she'd never said to anyone, not to her mother, not to Teo, ten feet away with his head in the furnace. Somewhere in nineteen years she'd stopped being sure he didn't do it. At fifteen she'd been sure. Now she wasn't, and she couldn't have said what year it changed.
At seventeen she'd asked a lawyer for help with it, once, and been told no. She remembered the no better than the lawyer.

Behind her, Teo's headlamp moved around inside the furnace closet. She looked at the page again and asked what a lawyer would ask. Why that witness? Why put a fifteen year old girl on the stand to talk about the laundry?
A. To show the jury the jacket was washed on the morning after the fight in the bar.
B. To have his own daughter tell the jury the jacket was washed out of routine.
C. To prove her father struck Travis Hensley while he was wearing that red jacket.
D. To establish the time she got home and fix the timeline of that morning.

She writes it out and has to stop. They didn't need her to say the jacket was in the washer. A detective could have said that. They needed her to say her mother did the laundry, on Mondays, and that she'd never once seen him do it. Coming from her, nobody could call it the State's story.

Good. That's how you read it. Primary purpose. Look at what the questions build: the jacket worn that day, found washed the next morning, by a man who never did laundry. And look at who's saying it. The purpose is to put that on the record through a witness nobody could call biased against him.

Teo packed up around ten. It's the sensor, not the igniter. I'll bring one tomorrow after work. He looked at the box one more time on his way to the stairs and didn't mention it, and she didn't mention the date.

The closing argument was further down, in a binder with a rubber band that broke when she touched it. She'd never read it. Witnesses weren't allowed in the courtroom after they testified, and by the time it was over she hadn't wanted to.

Trial transcript, Monday, June 9, 2008, the prosecution's closing argument. Consuelo Baca never saw a face. She told you that herself, and you can trust a witness who tells you what she didn't see. What she saw was a man in a red jacket strike Travis Hensley at a quarter past eleven and run. So who wore a red jacket that night? The defendant did. His own daughter told you he wore it to work that day. Ronnie Galvan told you the defendant and Travis fought inside the bar less than an hour before. The lab told you Travis Hensley's blood was on the cuff. And the next morning, before any officer knocked, that jacket was in the washer, in a house where he never did the laundry. The defendant told police he never touched anyone. The blood on his cuff says he did. People don't wash what they aren't worried about. Put it together, and the man in the red jacket was Luis Ruiz.

She read it once fast and once slow. His own daughter. Then she did it again, the one sentence version, because if she didn't make herself do something with it she was going to sit on the stairs all night.
Which choice best states the main point of the prosecutor's closing?
A. Consuelo Baca is a careful witness whose account the jury should trust completely.
B. Though the witness saw no face, the jacket evidence shows the man she saw was Luis.
C. The defendant lied to police when he told them he never touched Travis Hensley.
D. Washing the jacket proves Luis Ruiz knew he'd done something to Travis Hensley.

She writes it and looks at it. The closing admits the hole in its first sentence, no face, and then spends every other sentence filling it with a jacket. It's honest about the hole. That's what makes it work.

That's the one. Pencil down. Main idea. It covers the whole closing: the concession that Consuelo saw no face, and the claim that the jacket evidence closes that gap. A main idea often has this two part shape when a passage concedes something and then argues past it.
Decision five. What she didn't see.
One line kept pulling her back, the second one. You can trust a witness who tells you what she didn't see.

Dani had sat through enough trials since to know a prosecutor doesn't hand a jury a weakness for free. She'd never met Consuelo Baca. She'd seen her once in 2008, from the end of a hallway, a small woman in a church dress holding a little girl's hand. Whatever that line was doing, it was doing it on purpose.
A. To turn the missing face into a reason to trust her about the red jacket.
B. To admit a weakness in the State's case: its only eyewitness never saw a face.
C. To answer a defense claim that Consuelo Baca had lied to the police about that night.
D. To show the jury that Consuelo Baca had picked out Luis Ruiz as the man she saw.

She reads it again. It's a good line. It takes the hole in their case and makes it the reason to trust the rest of what Consuelo said, and the rest of what she said was a red jacket. For the first time Dani wonders what else Consuelo told the police that night that nobody asked her about at trial.

Right. Now say why. Function of a detail. The line concedes the weakness and converts it into credibility, which sets up the jacket in the next sentence. Function questions ask what a line is for, where it sits, not only what it says.

It was after eleven. She got a legal pad and drew the closing the way the book drew arguments: claims in boxes, arrows from each reason to whatever it held up. "The man in the red jacket was Luis Ruiz" went at the bottom of the page. The jacket, her testimony, the fight, and the blood went above it.
Then she got to the washer, and she didn't know where its box went. It was one sentence in the closing. At fifteen it had been the only thing anybody asked her about.
What role does the washer play in the closing?
A. It's the evidence that showed whose blood was on the cuff of the jacket that morning.
B. It's one of several premises offered directly to prove he was the man in red.
C. It's the conclusion the whole closing builds toward, the thing the jury had to find.
D. It backs the middle claim that he had something to hide, which backs the main one.

She draws a new box between the washer and the bottom line and writes in it: he was hiding something. The washer points at that box. That box points at her father. She looks at it a long time. The washer doesn't say anything about a parking lot. It only says something if you already think he was there.

Good. That's how you read it. Role of a statement. Ask what the sentence is for. The closing uses the washer to support "he was worried," and uses that to support "the man in red was Luis." A premise feeding an intermediate conclusion that feeds the main one: that's the job.

Wednesday, October 28, Teo came back after his shift with the sensor. The first cold night was supposed to be Friday. He'd brought a drawing from his daughter, Lupe, for the fridge. A purple horse. Or a dog. Lupe hadn't decided.

Seven o'clock, her phone. Wednesdays it always was, and she took it on the basement stairs. First the recording, same lady every week, where the call's from, that it's recorded. Dani could do the voice. Then her father, opening the way he'd opened every game since she was eight and their board came from a garage sale with a salt shaker for a rook. Mija. King's pawn, two squares. New game.
You always open with that. So you know where I'm going. Same as every time. Then, like it had just occurred to him, though he'd asked it every Wednesday for ten years: Is your brother there?

Teo had been half inside the furnace closet with a headlamp on when she came down at a quarter to seven. He'd looked at the clock on the water heater and backed out on his elbows. Sensor's in. You'll have heat Friday. Coat off the chair, out the back door, ten minutes early for nothing. His truck needed a muffler. She'd heard it to the corner.
He just left, Pa. Okay. He said it like he'd known before he asked. He usually had. Tell him I asked.

The last time those two were in a room together was Mom's viewing, 2016. Luis got an hour. Two officers at the back the whole time, everybody pretending they weren't there. At the casket Luis put his hand on Teo's shoulder (Teo was nineteen, already taller) and said something right into his ear. Dani was six feet off, holding her aunt's purse, and got none of it. After that Teo sat out in his truck till it was over. He never drove to Sterling again. She asked him once what Pa said. Nothing. She let it go. She was good at that.

I know what yesterday was, her father said. I'll say it once more, and then we play. I watched the game. Two beers. The place was full of Boston people in red, and there was pushing at the bar, everybody shoving. I never hit anybody. I left at a quarter to eleven, by myself, and your brother was at your Abuela's all night, thank God. A man got hurt out there. That's a terrible thing, and his family has a right to hate somebody for it. It wasn't me, mija. They needed a man in a red jacket, and I was standing there in one.
What's the main conclusion of her father's account?
A. That he left the bar by himself at a quarter to eleven, before anything happened.
B. That the State needed a man in a red jacket, and he was the one standing there.
C. That he wasn't the man who hurt Travis Hensley out in that lot. The rest backs that.
D. That Travis Hensley's family has every right in the world to hate somebody for it.

That it wasn't you, she says, so he knows she heard it. That's what all of it's for. He's quiet. That's what it's for. She notices he tells it the same way every time, in the same order, and that Teo comes into it only once, to be put at Abuela's.

That's the one. Pencil down. Main conclusion. "It wasn't me" is the claim the rest serves, and it's about the lot. "I never hit anybody" is about the bar. It's one of his reasons, like the two beers and the time he left. Find the sentence every other sentence is working for.
She told him she'd been reading the transcript.

Why would you read that, he said. Not a question. The washer. They made such a thing out of the washer. It was nothing, Dani. I spilled beer on it, your mother was at work, I put it in. A washing machine. They made a mountain out of a washing machine.
She could hear him smiling, the way he did when he wanted her to let something go. She'd let him, every Wednesday for years.
What job did the washer do in the State's case?
A. "It wasn't nothing to them, Pa. It made the blood on your cuff look like hiding."
B. "It was the whole case, Pa. Without the washer they wouldn't have had anything on you."
C. "It mattered that I'm the one who told them about it. They needed me to say it."
D. "You're right, Pa. A washer can't tell anybody who was out in that lot that night."

A few seconds of hiss on the line. Then: Your mother would've washed it Monday. I know. That's why it was a thing. He doesn't argue with her. He asks if it's cold in Commerce City yet, like Commerce City is another country.

Right. Now say why. Role of a statement. In the State's argument the washer backs "he had something to hide," and that claim is what turns blood from a bar fight into blood from a killing. Once you can name the job, you can answer him without agreeing and without a fight.
With a minute left on the call she'd given him her move, king's pawn, the answer she always gave. He'd laughed like it surprised him. It never did.

Wednesday at lunch she'd read her testimony again at her desk, which was a mistake, because Joel Harlan walked by. Thursday on the bus the prep book's reading set was about chess by mail, players who sent each other one move per letter for years. She thought about her father all the way downtown and got two questions wrong. Then her phone buzzed.
A text from Joel Harlan. Saw what you were reading at lunch yesterday. Come by before you do anything else with it. You're not in trouble. Joel

Joel was fifty two, the supervising attorney on her floor, and the man who'd written her a law school letter two years before she decided to apply. He closed his door, which he never did. Here's how it goes, he said. This office handled his appeal. If you find something, the first question anybody asks is whether his lawyers missed it, and some of those lawyers were ours. We can't be on both sides of that question. So...
He waited. He wanted her to say it.
Which completion follows most strongly from what Joel has said?
A. "So I keep it off the clock. Nights and weekends, after everybody's gone home."
B. "So none of it happens here. Not our files, not our hours, not our people."
C. "So I shouldn't talk about my father's case with anybody here in the office at all."
D. "So this office should take another look at it. We're the ones who handled it."

Joel nods. That's it. All of it, not just the hours. He opens his desk drawer and takes out an envelope with her name on it. Letter's still here. Whenever you want it. She doesn't take it yet. She doesn't say no, either.

Good. That's how you read it. Fill in the blank. The premises: the office represented him, and any new claim may say his earlier lawyers missed something. What follows is that the office can't be in it at all, and that's exactly what she says, no more.

The 2010 opinion had been in the box too, the Court of Appeals saying no in eleven pages. The lawyers' names were on the front. For the defendant, Ana Brennan, Deputy State Public Defender. Dani looked her up. Ana Brennan had gone into private practice in 2014. She had an office on Federal Boulevard, no website, and one phone number.

She called Friday. A woman answered on the first ring. Brennan. Dani gave her name, and her father's name, and the year. The pause was long enough that she thought the call had dropped. Monday, the woman said. Six o'clock. Bring the transcript. Leave the adjectives at home.

Monday, November 2, the laundromat on Federal was full of the evening wash, and the stairs up to the office smelled like dryer sheets. At the top: a desk, two chairs, a radiator, banker's boxes to the ceiling, and a gray greyhound asleep on a rug, who opened one eye and closed it again. A woman in her late fifties sat behind the desk sharpening a pencil with a pocketknife into the wastebasket.
That's Dicta, she said. She doesn't get up for anybody. Sit. Dani sat and started, My father was convicted in 2008 of... and Ana held up the pencil.
Stop. Before you tell me anything about him, tell me what the State concluded. One sentence. Not the verdict. The argument.
A. "That nobody else in that bar could have done it, so it had to be my father."
B. "That the jacket in the washer was the same jacket the man in the parking lot wore."
C. "That the man Consuelo Baca saw hit Travis at a quarter past eleven was my father."
D. "That my father killed a man, and then lied about it to everybody for nineteen years."
Ana writes it on a yellow pad, word for word, in pencil. Good. That's the only sentence they had to sell. Murder's the verdict. That's the argument. She points the pencil at Dani. Now I'll listen.

That's the one. Pencil down. Main conclusion. The verdict was murder, but the argument was about who. The jacket, the blood, the washer, and the daughter were all there to support one claim: the man the witness saw was Luis Ruiz.

Ana went through the transcript in maybe four minutes, licking her thumb for the pages. Dani's grandmother used to do that. Nobody else she knew. Page four, Ana stopped. Pencil point under one line: He wore it to work that day. I saw him leave in it.
This. What'd this do for them?
Dani's line. She'd known it would be since the bus.
A. "A premise. It put him in red that night, so he'd match what Consuelo saw."
B. "Nothing. Everybody already knew what he wore to work, so it didn't count."
C. "Their conclusion. Once he was in the jacket, the rest didn't really matter."
D. "A premise. It was the one that tied the blood on the cuff back to my father."

Ana nods. And it's true. She says it plainly, the way she'd say the time. Premises are supposed to be true. You did your part right. What they built on it is a different question. Dani has to look at the dog for a minute.

Right. Now say why. Role of a statement. Her line was given as true and supported by nothing. It held up the claim that Luis wore red that night, which the State used to match him to Consuelo's description. The premise was accurate. The trouble was the step after it.
Now you, Ana said. Tell me what's wrong with it. And don't you dare say everything.

She'd been working on it since Tuesday, on the bus, in the shower, on hold with the gas company. Consuelo saw a man in a red jacket. Every man on his crew wore that same jacket, and half the city was in Red Sox red that night. So the jacket...
She stopped. Ana waited with the pencil up.
Which ending is properly supported by what she's said so far?
A. "...proves my father isn't the man she saw that night."
B. "...was never really evidence of anything at all."
C. "...can't tell you which of those men in red she saw."
D. "...means the police should've looked at Boston fans."
Ana writes it under the first sentence. Reads both out loud, flat, like a grocery list. That's the case. Not the washer. Not the blood. That.

Good. That's how you read it. Fill in the blank. The premises say the description fits many men, and what they earn is that it can't single out one of them. Notice what it doesn't say. Nothing about innocence. Only that the jacket can't hold what the State hung on it.

Dark on Federal by then. A dryer buzzed downstairs and somebody laughed at it. Ana leaned back, chair creaking like it had opinions, and looked at Dani over the pad. Didn't say anything. Kept not saying it.
Do you think he did it?
Dani didn't answer that. On the rug Dicta stood up, turned one circle, and lay down again in the same spot, facing the other way.

All right, Ana said. That'll do for a first night. People climb those stairs and tell me their father's innocent, and mostly I can't help them, because what they want is for me to agree. I don't agree with anybody. I read.
Ana asked where the papers came from. A box in my basement. My mother kept everything. Ana nodded like that was the best answer she'd heard all week. Mothers usually do.
You found the conclusion before you went looking for the flaw, Ana said, to the pad more than to Dani. Most lawyers can't do that. Most lawyers don't try.

No money. She said that first, like it was a condition. What she wanted was Tuesday and Thursday nights, every other Saturday, and Dani wrong out loud whenever Dani was wrong. And you keep your test date. I won't be the reason you don't go to law school. Top drawer, then.

A stapled copy of something came out, folded and unfolded so often it had gone soft as a dish towel. Dani knew the first page. She had one just like it in the box. The 2010 opinion. Hers she'd read twice, both times on the basement stairs. Ana's had pencil all down the margins and a coffee ring on the back.
Ana put it on top of the transcript. Squared the corners. Left her hand on it.
Don't tell me he's innocent, she said. Tell me what they had to believe.
